en: The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra in Five Sections, Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Minghui of Jianchu Monastery during the Liang Dynasty.
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen! Of the first month of spring, one night has passed and only one night remains."
The moon is waning;
old age and death have drawn near, and the Buddha-dharma is about to perish. Sisters!
For the sake of attaining the Way, one should practice with single-minded diligence and vigor. Why is this?
Because it was through single-minded diligence and vigor that all Buddhas attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; how much more so for other wholesome dharmas of the Path!
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
I now wish to recite the precepts, and the Saṃgha should listen with a single mind.
Even regarding minor offenses, one’s heart should feel great dread.
If you have committed an offense, repent with a single-minded heart; henceforth, do not commit it again.
The horse of the mind gallops toward evil paths, and its heedlessness is difficult to restrain;
the Buddha taught the practice of earnest precepts, which are like sharp reins and bits.
The Buddha speaks words of instruction; those who are virtuous can believe and accept them.
Such a person is like a well-trained horse, able to defeat the army of afflictions.
But if one does not receive his instructions, nor cherish the precepts, [one remains bound].
Such a person has neither tamed their horse nor subdued themselves, and they are submerged in the army of afflictions.
If a person guards the precepts as a yak loves its tail,
binding the mind with heedfulness like a monkey bound by chains.
"By constantly exerting oneself day and night for the sake of seeking true wisdom,
such a person within the Buddha-dharma is able to attain a pure livelihood.
"Those who have not received full ordination, please leave."
If there is someone present, she should be sent away according to her words; if there is no one, she should reply:
"There is no one here who has not yet received full ordination. "Sisters!..."
"Let those bhikṣuṇīs who have not arrived announce their *chanda* and purification.
Those who are present speak according to their words; those who are absent reply, "There is no one here to announce their *chanda*."
“The Saṃgha is now in harmony; what should be done first?
He replied, “The formal act (karmavācanā) for reciting the Prātimokṣa.”
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts; the Sangha shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts with one mind.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen."
The announcement is thus made. "Sisters!
Now we shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*. All of you listen together and reflect upon it well."
If there is any offense, it should be confessed; those who are without offense should remain silent.
By your silence, you should know that I and the elder sisters are pure.
As with the noble silence, so it is with me and the elder sisters.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when thus addressed three times in the midst of the community, remembers having committed an offense but does not disclose it, she incurs the offense of intentional lying.
The Buddha has declared that the offense of intentional lying is an obstructive dharma.
"To disclose [one's transgressions] brings peace and happiness; not to disclose them causes the offense to deepen.
"Sisters, the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra has been recited."
"Now I ask, sisters, are you pure in this matter?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "Sisters, you are pure in this matter, for you are silent; it shall be held as such."
“Sisters! These eight *pārājika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

‘If a bhikṣuṇī, who has trained together with other bhikṣuṇīs in the rules of the precepts, should engage in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—while her precepts are weak and she has not relinquished them, this bhikṣuṇī commits a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.’”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given with a thieving mind—whether a king or a high minister seizes her, binds her, kills her, or banishes her, saying:
'You are a thief! You are a petty person! You are a fool!'"
This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether it be a human or one who resembles a human, kills by her own hand, or kills by providing a weapon or poison, or instructs another to kill, or instructs someone to commit suicide, or praises death and extols death, saying:
'Alas, person! What is the use of living such an evil life?'"
"Death is better than life.

With such a thought, she follows her intention and kills; through various causes and conditions such as these, because of this [intention], he dies. This bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without knowing or seeing the superhuman state—the noble, beneficial, and perfected—claims for herself: 'I know thus; I see thus.'"
Later, whether that bhikṣuṇī is questioned or not, for the sake of purifying herself by confessing her offense, she speaks thus:
"I said I knew what I did not know, and I said I saw what I did not see; it was a false and deceptive lie."
"Excepting those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in communion.

If a bhikṣuṇī, her mind transformed by the intensity of lust, consents to various kinds of touching by a man—from below the hairline to above the knees and behind the elbows—this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in communion."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, her mind transformed by the intensity of lust, consents to a man’s grasping her hand, grasping her robe, meeting him alone in private, traveling with him alone, staying with him alone, conversing with him alone, sitting on the same seat with him, or physically drawing near to a man."
One who possesses these eight factors is a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has lawfully performed the *ajñapti-karman* of 'not seeing an offense' against a bhikṣu—whereby the bhikṣus do not dwell with him, do not perform affairs with him, and do not speak with him—yet follows and sides with him."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister!

This community of bhikṣus has already performed the *karma* of not seeing one's offense against you; the bhikṣus do not dwell with you, do not perform affairs with you, and do not converse with you. Do not follow their lead."
If, after being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish her position, she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If she relinquishes the matter after the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense and conceals it,

and at a later time— whether that [other] bhikṣuṇī is still present, has died, has gone far away, has been expelled, has left the order, or has changed her appearance— the [concealing] bhikṣuṇī speaks thus:
'I previously saw with my own eyes her committing a pārājika offense.'"
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion. "Sisters,
the eight pārājika dharmas have now been recited."
If a bhikṣuṇī violates any one of these precepts, she may not live in community with the others.
As it was before, so it is after; such a bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense and should not be lived with.
Now I ask: "Are you all pure in this matter, sisters?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "Since you are silent, sisters, you are pure in this matter; let it be so held."
“Sisters! These seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra.

‘If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a matchmaker for illicit affairs, conveying a man’s intent to a woman or a woman’s intent to a man, even resulting in a single act of sexual intercourse, this bhikṣuṇī has committed her first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.’”

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of an improper and malicious anger, should falsely accuse with groundless charges of a pārājika offense a bhikṣuṇī who has not committed a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy her holy life."
If, at a later time, whether questioned or unasked, that bhikṣuṇī says:
"This matter of mine was groundless; I slandered out of a state of anger," then that bhikṣuṇī has committed an initial *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of an improper and malicious anger, takes a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a different category [of offense] and, with the intent to destroy another's holy life, falsely accuses a bhikṣuṇī who has not committed a pārājika offense of having committed a pārājika offense."
At a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣuṇī says:
"In this matter, I took a fragment or something resembling a fragment from among dissimilar categories; I slandered her out of a state of anger."
"This nun has committed her first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.

If a nun, knowing that a woman with an offense has not been permitted by her guardian, ordains her as a member of the Path—excepting one who had previously gone forth—this nun has committed her first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has lawfully expelled another bhikṣuṇī who is not yet tamed in mind and does not comply with the Saṃgha, should herself, together with her followers, resolve that expulsion outside the boundary, this bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed."
“If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps alone, crosses water alone, or stays behind alone on a road while feeling lustful attachment toward a man—
except when there is a valid reason— this bhikṣuṇī has committed an initial *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that requires confession.”

As for "circumstances" (nidāna): when fleeing in fear; when one is so exhausted by old age or illness that one cannot keep pace with one's companions; at a place where the water is narrow and shallow and there are bridges or boats; or in a place where one fears men—these are called circumstances.
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to an official court and speaks on behalf of another person, this bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of attachment, receives food from the hand of a man who has a mind of attachment and eats it, this bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed."
"If a bhikṣuṇī instructs another bhikṣuṇī, saying: 'You need only refrain from giving rise to defiled attachment;
what harm is there in accepting food and drink from a man who is defiled by attachment?'"
This nun has committed her first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.
"If a nun exerts herself in skillful means for the purpose of breaking a harmonious Saṃgha..."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not strive with skillful means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha.

Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, it is joyful and free from strife; with one mind and one training, like water and milk mixed together, you shall jointly propagate the Teacher’s instruction and dwell in peace and happiness."
"If she is thus admonished and persists in not relinquishing [the matter], she should be admonished a second and third time.
If she relinquishes the matter upon the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense which is to be confessed."
"If a bhikṣuṇī assists in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha—whether it be one, two, or many—and says to the other bhikṣuṇīs:

'What this bhikṣuṇī says is said with knowledge, not without knowledge; she speaks of the Dharma, not of what is not Dharma; she speaks of the Vinaya, not of what is not Vinaya; all of this is what our hearts accept and delight in.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī: "Do not speak these words:

'What this bhikṣuṇī has spoken was spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge; she spoke the Dharma, not what is not Dharma; she spoke the Vinaya, not what is not Vinaya; all of this is what our hearts accept and delight in.'"
Why is this? This bhikṣuṇī does not speak with knowledge, she does not speak the Dharma, nor does she speak the Vinaya; do not take pleasure in assisting in the breaking of the harmony of the Saṃgha.

One should joyfully assist in bringing the Saṃgha into harmony; because the Saṃgha is harmonious, there is joy and no contention. With a single mind and a single training, like water and milk blending together, they shall collectively propagate the Teacher’s instruction and dwell in peace and happiness.
If, after being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If she relinquishes the matter upon the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must undergo confession.
"If a bhikṣuṇī is of an evil disposition and difficult to converse with,
and repeatedly commits offenses while training together with the other bhikṣuṇīs in the Sūtra on the Precepts (Śīla-sūtra),
and the bhikṣuṇīs admonish her regarding her transgressions in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya."
He replied:
"Auntie! Do not speak to me of what is good or bad, nor shall I speak to you of what is good or bad."
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to her again, saying:
"Do not act as one who is self-centered and refuses to converse with others.
You should speak in accordance with the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs shall likewise speak in accordance with the Dharma for your sake."
"In this way, by teaching one another in succession and helping one another emerge from their offenses, you shall become the Saṃgha of the Tathāgata.
If, despite being thus admonished, he persists and does not relinquish his position, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she abandons this matter, it is well.
If she does not abandon it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense which is to be confessed.

"If a bhikṣuṇī resides in dependence upon a village and engages in evil conduct that defiles families, such that her evil conduct is seen, heard, and known by all, and her defiling of families is likewise seen, heard, and known; [and if she does not abandon it, she commits an offense of expiation]."
The other bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī:
"You have committed evil conduct and defiled families; your evil conduct has been seen, heard, and known by all, and your defiling of families has also been seen, heard, and known."
"Go away; you should not remain here. That bhikṣuṇī said:
"The elder sisters follow after desire, hatred, delusion, and fear."
"Why is this? Among bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses, some are expelled while others are not.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke further, saying:
"Do not speak these words:
'The elder nuns speak according to favoritism, anger, delusion, and fear;
there are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed equal offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not.'"
"You have engaged in misconduct and defiled families; your misconduct has been seen, heard, and known, and your defilement of families has also been seen, heard, and known.
You must abandon these words spoken out of attachment, aversion, delusion, or fear."
"Depart from here; you should not remain in this place.
If, despite being thus admonished, he persists and does not relinquish [his position], he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, upon the second and third admonition, he relinquishes this matter, it is well.
If she does not relinquish [the behavior], that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that may be confessed.
"If two bhikṣuṇīs together engage in evil conduct and have an evil reputation, and they further conceal each other's offenses and cause vexation to the Saṃgha..."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to them:
"You two bhikṣuṇīs have committed evil deeds together and have acquired an evil reputation; you have covered for one another's offenses and caused distress to the Saṃgha."
"You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these evil deeds and matters of provoking the Saṃgha, and dwell in peace and security within the Buddha-dharma.
Those two bhikṣuṇīs said:
"We have committed no evil acts, nor do we have an evil reputation; we have not concealed our offenses, nor have we provoked the Saṃgha."
"Furthermore, there are two other bhikṣuṇīs here who together commit evil deeds and cause distress to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke again, saying: "Do not speak such words."
Why is this? Because within this community there are no other two bhikṣuṇīs who commit evil acts to harass the Saṃgha, save for yourselves.
You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these evil deeds and the acts of provoking the Saṃgha, and so dwell in peace, increasing and expanding within the Buddha-dharma.
If, after being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If she relinquishes the matter upon the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense which is to be confessed.
"If two bhikṣuṇīs together commit evil deeds and acquire an evil reputation, and they further conceal each other's offenses, thereby causing vexation to the Saṃgha.
Other bhikṣuṇīs should say to them:
'You two bhikṣuṇīs have together committed evil deeds and acquired an evil reputation; you further conceal each other's offenses and cause vexation to the Saṃgha.'"
"You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these evil deeds and matters of provoking the Saṃgha, and dwell in peace and security within the Buddha’s Dharma.
The two bhikṣuṇīs said, "We have committed no evil deeds, nor do we have an evil reputation; we have not concealed our offenses, nor have we provoked the Saṃgha."
"The monks see that we are weak and, treating us with contempt,
speak such words. The bhikṣuṇīs replied again,
"Do not say such things."
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha does not see you as weak and treats you with contempt.

You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these acts of wrongdoing and the matters that cause distress to the Saṃgha, and thus increase your progress within the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness.
If, despite being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish it, a second and third admonition should be given.
If she relinquishes the matter after the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense that must be confessed.
"If a bhikṣuṇī is fond of quarreling with others,
and the Saṃgha has adjudicated the matter, she then says:
'The Saṃgha acts out of favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Do not take pleasure in quarreling with others.
Do not speak such words."
"The Sangha follows desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
Why is this? Because the Sangha does not follow desire, hatred, delusion, or fear.
"You should abandon these words; by doing so, you will increase and broaden your practice within the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace.
If, despite being admonished in this way, they persistently refuse to abandon them, they should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she abandons this matter, it is well.
If she does not abandon it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense that must be confessed.
"If a bhikṣuṇī is fond of quarreling with others, and the Saṃgha has settled the matter, she then says:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha, and I renounce the precepts; I shall become a follower of an external path.'"
"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas also train in the precepts and possess a sense of shame; I can practice the holy life under them.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her, "Do not take pleasure in quarreling with others."
Do not speak these words:
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Why is this?
Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas lack the training of one beyond learning and are devoid of shame and remorse.
How can you practice the holy life under them?
Abandon this evil view; within the Buddha’s Dharma, you shall increase and expand, attaining a state of peaceful dwelling.
"If she is thus admonished and yet persists in not relinquishing [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If she relinquishes the matter upon the second or third admonition, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense which is to be confessed."
"Venerable Sisters! The seventeen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas have been recited: nine offenses that are complete from the first moment of commission, and eight that require up to three admonitions.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these offenses, she must undergo *mānatva* for half a month within the two divisions of the Saṃgha; thereafter, she proceeds to *ābhāṣaṇā*."

Once the procedure has been performed according to the Dharma, the offense must be cleared before each of the two assemblies of monks, with at least twenty members in each; if even one person is missing, it is not called "clearing the offense," and the bhikṣuṇīs may also censure the monks.
"This is the nature of this Dharma.
Now I ask: Are you pure in this matter, sisters?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "Since you are silent, sisters, you are pure in this matter. Thus shall this matter be held."
“Sisters! These thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra*.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her five robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* cloth, keeps an extra robe for up to ten days...’”
If she exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished making her robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* privileges, should stay apart from any one of her five robes for even one night—unless there has been a formal authorization (*saṃgha-karman*) by the Saṃgha—it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, obtains an out-of-season robe, she should accept it if she needs it, and quickly have it made up and taken possession of."
If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, one may hope for further acquisition from other sources to make it complete, even up to one month.
If this period is exceeded, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī requests a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except when there is a valid cause, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
A 'valid cause' refers to: having one's robes taken away, lost, burned, carried away by water, or destroyed; these are called valid causes."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having had her robes stolen, lost, burned, washed away, or destroyed, begs for robes from a householder or housewife who is not a relative. [If she does so, she commits an offense. "
If a householder or a householder’s wife wishes to give many robes, that bhikṣuṇī should accept two robes; if she accepts more than that, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has deliberated together, saying:
“We shall use this price for cloth to make a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī,” and that bhikṣuṇī,
having not previously received an invitation to choose [the gift], goes to the householder or householder’s wife and says:
"Will you make a robe for me from this amount of cloth for robes? He replied, "I will."
He then said: "Excellent, householder! Excellent, householder's wife!"
‘You should make such and such a robe for me, so that it may be fine,’ [the nun incurs] a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
‘If a householder or a householder’s wife who are not relatives have consulted together:’
"I shall each have robes made from such an amount of money for the purpose of giving them to a certain bhikṣuṇī.
Without having previously received a formal invitation, that bhikṣuṇī goes to the layman or the housewife and asks:
"Are you each having robes made for me from such an amount of money?"
He replied, "So it is. Then he said:
"Excellent, householder and housewife!
You may join together to provide me with a single robe, for the sake of its excellence."
" [This constitutes] a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a king, a great minister, a brahmin, or a householder, for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, sends a messenger to deliver the value of a robe."
The messenger went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said,
"Ayyās! That king and his ministers have sent this money for the purchase of robes."
"Āryā, please accept it. That bhikṣuṇī said,
"I should not accept the price for robes."
"If you obtain a pure robe, you should receive and hold it with your own hands.
The messenger said, "Ayyā!"
"Is there anyone in charge?
The bhikṣuṇī then pointed out the location.
The messenger went to where the person in charge was and said:
"A certain king or minister has sent the price for this robe to such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī.
Please accept it on her behalf and have it made.
He then gave it to her.
Having given it to the official, the messenger returned to the bhikṣuṇī and said: "Ayyā!
I have finished giving what you indicated to the official."
“Sister, if you need robes, you may go and take them.
That bhikṣuṇī went to the place where the official was three times, saying each time:
“I need robes.”
"I require robes.
If he obtains them, that is well.
If he does not obtain them, he should go before the attendant four times, five times, or six times and stand there in silence. If he obtains them, that is well.
If she should seek to obtain it beyond this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she does not obtain the robe, she should go to the place from which the messenger came, or go herself, or send a message, saying:
"The price for a robe was sent by you for the sake of such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī; yet that bhikṣuṇī has not obtained it at all."
"You must go yourself to reclaim it; do not let it be lost.
This matter should be handled in this way.
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself begs for thread and hires a weaver to weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a householder or a householder's wife has employed a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣuṇī,
and that bhikṣuṇī, having not been previously invited by them, goes to the weaver's workshop and says:
'Do you know this?'"
"This robe is being made for me.
For my sake, you must weave it well so that it is extremely fine and wide; I shall reward you separately.
If, afterwards, she receives a meal or the value of a meal [for this], it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
10. "If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe to another bhikṣuṇī, and later, being angry and displeased, either takes it back herself or causes someone else to take it back, saying:
'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
“[This constitutes] a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it for her own personal use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.’”
"If a bhikṣuṇī is ill, she may take four kinds of medicinal substances for internal consumption—
clarified butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar— for up to seven days after a single acceptance."
If she exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, during the preceding or following retreat (*pūrvavarṣā* or *paścimavarṣā*), when ten days remain before the *pravāraṇā*, receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), she may accept it if she needs it, until the time for robes [has passed]."
If she exceeds this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when her bowl has not yet reached five mends, should seek a new bowl for the sake of its beauty, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of trade for the sake of profit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī buys and sells gold, silver, or money in various ways, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes hold of gold, silver, or money, or causes another to take them, or forms the intention to accept them, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
“If a bhikṣuṇī first requests this [material], but having received it does not use it, and instead requests another thing, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī accepts out-of-season robe-cloth as in-season robe-cloth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.”
20. "If a bhikṣuṇī exchanges a robe with another bhikṣuṇī and later regrets it and demands it back, she commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense upon obtaining [the robe]."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when other bhikṣuṇīs say to her,
'Take this menstrual cloth,' says to herself:"
"It is not permitted.
To take it beforehand at that time constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī requests heavy robes, she should accept those worth four *kārṣāpaṇa*s in value."
"If one receives a garment of high value, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī begs for light clothing, she should accept that which is worth two and a half large coins."
If one receives a robe of high value, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of the Saṃgha and for this purpose, begs from a single lay devotee [for a robe], yet uses it for another purpose, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of the Saṃgha and for this specific purpose, begs from many lay devotees, yet uses it for another purpose, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, for her own sake, begs from a layperson for this purpose but uses it for another purpose herself, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, for her own sake, begs from many householders for this purpose, yet uses it for another purpose herself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī hoards or accumulates utensils, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī accumulates many alms bowls, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"Venerable sisters! The thirty *niḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas have been recited.
Now I ask: Are you pure in regard to these matters?"
A second and third time, it should be said in the same way: "Sisters, you are pure in this matter, for you remain silent;
thus shall this matter be upheld. "Sisters!..."
These two hundred and ten *pāyattika* rules are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*:
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks a deliberate falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī reviles another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī uses double-tongued speech to cause dissension among bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī preaches the Dharma to a man for more than five or six sentences, except when there is a woman present who understands the difference between good and bad speech, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has already settled a matter in accordance with the Dharma, should reopen it, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī teaches a woman who has not yet received full ordination the sūtras, and recites them together with her, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a woman who has not received full ordination for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks to a woman who has not received full ordination about having attained superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
If it is true, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing of a bhikṣuṇī’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), speaks of it to a woman who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (*saṃghakamma*), it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: ‘What is the use of these minor rules?
When these rules are recited, they cause people distress.’”
To disparage the precepts in such a manner constitutes a *pāyattika* offense. Ten:
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself cuts down a 'village of spirits' (*bhūtagrāma*), or causes another to cut it down, saying, 'Cut this down,' it is a *pāyattika* offense."
“If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally does not answer when questioned, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī falsely accuses a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having personally spread out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha on an open space, or having had someone else spread it, or if it has been spread by another, sits or lies down upon it;
and when departing, does not herself put it away, nor instructs another to put it away, nor entrusts it to someone to be put away, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, within a monastery dwelling, spreads out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha herself, or causes another to spread it, or sits or lies down upon it when it has been spread by another."
If, when departing, she does not lift up [the bedding] herself, nor instructs another to lift it up, nor entrusts someone to lift it up, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, personally drags a bhikṣuṇī out of the saṃghārāma, or causes another to drag her out, saying these words:
'Get out! Be gone! Do not stay here.'"
“[This constitutes] a *pāyattika*.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has already spread bedding, later comes and forcibly spreads it herself or causes someone else to spread it, thinking:
“If they do not like it, they shall leave of their own accord.”’”
"An offense of expiation (pāyattika).
If a bhikṣuṇī sits or lies down with force upon a rope bed or wooden bed with pointed legs on an upper story of a multi-storied monastery building, it is an offense of expiation."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living organisms, takes it for the purpose of pouring on mud, or for food and drink, or for any other use, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats repeatedly, except when there is a specific cause, it is a pāyattika.”
Regarding the "circumstances": the time of illness, the time of making robes, and the time of being offered robes—these are called the circumstances.
Twenty: "If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for a communal meal from individuals, except in the case of the aforementioned circumstances, it is a pāyattika."

Regarding "circumstances": the time of illness, the time of receiving robes, the time of making robes, the time of traveling on a road, traveling by boat, and the time of a great assembly—these are called circumstances.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, accepts more than one meal at a place where food is being given, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the home of a layperson and they offer her food and drink freely, whether cakes or parched grain flour...”
If one does not eat at that person's home, one should accept two or three bowls; having gone outside, one should eat together with other bhikṣuṇīs.
If one is not ill and accepts more than this, or does not eat together with other bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her meal, eats food without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) procedure, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her meal, does not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* procedure, yet forcibly urges another to eat with the intent to cause them to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī places food in her mouth that has not been formally offered, except for tasting food, tooth-sticks, and water, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats leftover food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits with a man inside a house where a meal is being served, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī observes an army setting out on a march, it is a pāyattika.
Thirty: If a bhikṣuṇī has a reason to go into an army, she may stay there for two or three nights."
If she exceeds [the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having a reason, stays in an army for two or three nights, and observes the military formations or the engagement of battle, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: 'As I understand the Buddha's teaching,
the dharmas that obstruct the path cannot obstruct the path,' the other bhikṣuṇīs should say to that bhikṣuṇī:"
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Buddha, do not misrepresent the Buddha.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha as obstructive to the Path truly can obstruct the Path.
You must abandon this evil and false view."
When he is thus admonished and yet persists in his refusal to relinquish [the matter], he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, upon the second and third admonition, he relinquishes this matter, it is well.
If she does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has not repented according to the Dharma and has not relinquished her evil and heterodox views, should dwell with her, converse with her, sleep with her, or engage in affairs with her, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a śrāmaṇerikā should speak these words:
'As I understand what the Buddha has taught, if one experiences the five desires,
they cannot obstruct the Path,' the bhikṣuṇīs should say to that śrāmaṇerikā:"
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Buddha, do not misrepresent the Buddha.
The Buddha has said that the five desires obstruct the Path and truly are able to obstruct the Path.
You, śrāmaṇerī, must abandon this evil and false view."
"If he is thus instructed and persists in not relinquishing it, he should be instructed a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third instructions, he relinquishes this matter, it is well."
If she does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should say to this śrāmaṇerī:
"Leave! From now on, do not say that the Buddha is your teacher, and do not walk behind the bhikṣuṇīs."
"Whereas other śrāmaṇerīs are permitted to stay together with the bhikṣuṇīs for two nights, you have no such privilege.
You fool, get out! Be gone! Do not remain here."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerī has been legally expelled, keeps her, employs her, lives with her, or speaks with her, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally causes another bhikṣuṇī to experience doubt and regret, thinking:
'I shall cause this bhikṣuṇī to be troubled, even if only for a short time.'"
“[If a bhikṣuṇī] does so, it is a pāyattika.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha is conducting its business, rises and leaves without having given her consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika.
‘If a bhikṣuṇī tickles another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.’”
"If a bhikṣuṇī plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
Forty: 'If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika.'"
“If a bhikṣuṇī drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī treats her teacher with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth herself, or causes another to dig it, saying ‘Dig this,’ it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, after a dispute has occurred, listens in silence with the thought:
'I shall remember what these bhikṣuṇīs say,' it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*, and accepts it beyond that period—except in the case of a renewed invitation, a personally delivered invitation, or a permanent invitation—it is a *pāyattika* offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī repeatedly commits offenses and the other bhikṣuṇīs admonish her in accordance with the Dharma,
yet she speaks thus:
'I will not train in this precept.'"
"You should ask other bhikṣuṇīs who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya.
This constitutes a pāyattika offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, speaks as follows:"
"I have only now learned that this Dharma was taught in the *Upoṣadha-Śīla-Sūtra*.
The bhikṣuṇīs knew that this bhikṣuṇī had already sat through the recitation of the precepts two or three times.
This bhikṣuṇī cannot escape by claiming ignorance; she shall be dealt with according to the law in accordance with the offense committed. Her ignorance should be rebuked thus:
"What you have done is unwholesome; when the precepts were recited, you did not listen with a single-minded focus, nor did you take them to heart."
“An *pāyattika*. ‘If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a thief to travel together on a road, from one village to another village, it is an *pāyattika*.’”
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a man to travel together along a road, from one village to another, it is a pāyattika.
Fifty: "If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, kindles a fire or causes someone else to kindle one for the purpose of warming herself, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes, or causes another to take, precious objects or similar items, except within a monastery or a lodging, it is a pāyattika."
If one takes precious objects or the like from within a monastic dwelling or a lodging, they must be returned when the owner later comes to claim them;
this matter should be handled in this way.
"If a bhikṣuṇī bathes within the interval of half a month, except for a special cause, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding "circumstances": the time of illness, the time of work, the time of traveling on a road, the time of wind and rain, and the time of heat—these are called circumstances.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, makes a threatening gesture with her hand toward another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally terrifies a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, slanders another bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
'Come together to various households; I will give you much delicious food and drink.'"
Having arrived, he did not give [the seat] and spoke thus: "Go away.
It is neither pleasant for me to sit or speak with you; it is pleasant for me to sit alone and speak alone."
If she does so out of a desire to cause annoyance, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī has new robes, they should be marked with three colors—either blue, black, or madder."
If one does not make a mark with the three colors, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of amusement, hides another bhikṣuṇī’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, or any such individual article of daily life, or causes another to hide them, it is a *pāyattika*."
60. "If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha is deciding a matter, has already formally given her consent (*chanda*) in accordance with the Dharma, and later reviles it again, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: 'The bhikṣuṇīs give away Saṃgha property to those they know,' [it is a *pāyattika*]."
"An *pāyattika*. 'If a bhikṣuṇī, having given a pure gift of clothing to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, forcibly takes it back, it is an *pāyattika*.'"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having accepted an invitation, goes from house to house before or after a meal without informing another bhikṣuṇī who is nearby, except for a specific reason."
A *pāyattika*. Regarding the causal basis: "the time for robes" is what is meant by the causal basis.
"If a bhikṣuṇī fills a seat or bed with *tūla* (cotton down), it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes for herself a rope bed or a wooden bed for sitting or lying upon, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Sugata, excluding the space where they enter the frame.
If they exceed this, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes a robe according to the measure of the Sugata’s robe, or exceeds it, it is a pāyattika.”
Regarding the measurement of a Sugata-cīvara: it is nine Sugata-spans in length and six spans in width; this is called the measurement of a Sugata-cīvara.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a donor intends to give an object to the Saṃgha, diverts it to another person, she commits a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.
Seventy: If a bhikṣuṇī slaps her female organ with her hand, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī inserts the male organ into the female organ, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī washes the female organ with water, she should use two fingers, limited to the first joint."
If she exceeds [the limit], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair from her armpits or private parts, it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands or converses in a secluded place alone with a bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī stands or converses alone in a secluded place with a layperson or a follower of another sect, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī stands or converses alone in an exposed place with a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands or converses in a secluded place with a layperson or a member of another sect, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands or whispers in a secluded alleyway with a bhikṣu, having sent away her companion bhikṣuṇī so that she is far removed, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands alone in a narrow alley with a layperson or a follower of another sect and whispers to them, having sent away her companion bhikṣuṇī to a distance, it is a pāyattika."
80. “If a bhikṣuṇī bathes naked, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī goes away from the water while wearing her bathing robe, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having received a new robe from another bhikṣuṇī, first offers it as an act of veneration and then does not return it, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī obstructs the distribution of robes by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having set aside a bhikṣuṇī’s robe, does not complete it within four or five days when she is not ill, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels separated from her five robes, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives a bhikṣuṇī’s robe to a layperson or a female follower of another sect, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intercepts an item intended as a gift for an individual and gives it to the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, out of favoritism, protects a family, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī does not observe the rains retreat, it is a pāyattika.
Ninety: “If a bhikṣuṇī does not observe the rains retreat in dependence upon the community of bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī travels during the rainy season retreat, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy season retreat, does not request the saṃgha of bhikṣus to address any offenses she has seen, heard, or suspected, it is an offense of expiation.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed her invitation for the rainy season retreat, does not depart after staying for one night, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels alone through a region within the country that is dangerous and where there is no one to rely upon, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels alone through a border region or a place of danger without anyone to rely upon, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rains retreat, departs for travel without entrusting the vihāra to someone else, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rains retreat, does not relinquish the vihāra to its owner before departing, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes about sightseeing in various ways, it is a pāyattika."
101. “If a bhikṣuṇī does not request an instructor from the Saṃgha every half-month, it is a pāyattika. 102.
“If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dwelling where bhikṣus reside and sees a bhikṣu, she must announce her presence; except in times of emergency or distress, it is a pāyattika.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a retinue when she has not yet reached twelve years [of seniority], it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has reached twelve years [of seniority] keeps a retinue without the Saṃgha having granted her the formal act (karmavācanā) for keeping a retinue, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon an unmarried girl who is less than twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a married girl who is twelve years of age or older, without the Saṃgha having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers the training precepts upon a girl who is less than eighteen years of age, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, even though the girl is eighteen years of age, confers the training precepts upon her without the Saṃgha having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to a laywoman: 'First give me a robe, and I shall ordain you,' it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to other bhikṣuṇīs: 'As the Buddha has taught, you should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for her to maintain a group of followers;
however, you do not possess this quality.'"
"If a bhikṣuṇī scolds other bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not go to listen when instruction or a formal ritual (karmavācanā) is being performed, it is a pāyattika."
110. "If a bhikṣuṇī does not grant full ordination to a śikṣamāṇā who has completed two years of training and is free from obstacles, but instead says to her:

One should train in receiving food without overflowing the bowl."
"One should train oneself: 'One shall eat both the soup and the rice together.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not take food from various places within the bowl.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not scoop out the center of the bowl while eating.'"
"One should train oneself not to eat by wiping the bowl with a bent finger.
One should train oneself not to eat by sniffing at the food.
One should train oneself to look attentively at the food in the bowl."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not discard food or drink.
One should train oneself: 'With hands soiled by food, one shall not grasp a vessel for pure drink.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not slurp while eating.'"
"One should train oneself not to make noise while chewing food.
One should train oneself not to lick the bowl for food.
One should train oneself not to take up a full handful of food."
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not eat with my mouth wide open.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not wait with my mouth open until the rice has arrived.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not stuff my cheeks while eating.'"
"One should train oneself not to bite off half a morsel of food.
One should train oneself not to eat with the nose wrinkled.
One should train oneself not to speak while food is in the mouth."
70. “One should train oneself not to reach out one’s arm to take food.
One should train oneself not to shake one’s hand while eating.
One should train oneself not to lick the food with the tongue.”
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not swallow food whole.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not take morsels of food and cast them into the mouth from afar.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not sprinkle water containing food from my bowl onto the interior of a layperson's house.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not disparage or criticize the food.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not request additional food for myself.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not look at the bowl of my neighbor with a mind of disdain.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not defecate or urinate in pure water, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself not to defecate or urinate upon living grass or vegetables, except when ill.
One should train oneself not to preach the Dharma to a person wearing shoes, except when ill."
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person wearing leather sandals, except when they are ill; this is a training to be observed.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person exposing their chest, except when they are ill; this is a training to be observed."
"One should train oneself: 'If a person is seated and a bhikṣuṇī is standing, one should not preach the Dharma to her, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'If a person is on a high seat and a bhikṣuṇī is on a lower one, one should not preach the Dharma to her, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: 'When a person is lying down and a bhikṣuṇī is sitting, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: 'When a person is in front and a bhikṣuṇī is behind, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.'"
90. “One should train oneself: ‘If a person is on the road and a bhikṣuṇī is off the road, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: ‘One should not preach the Dharma to a person with their head covered, except in the case of illness.’”
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who has their robe draped over one shoulder, except when ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to one who has their robe draped over both shoulders, except when ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is covering their body with a cloak.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is mounted on a vehicle.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one leaning on a staff, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not preach the Dharma to one holding a sword, except when they are ill.'"
"One should train oneself: 'I shall not teach the Dharma to a person holding a bow and arrow, except when they are ill.
One should train oneself: 'I shall not climb a tree higher than a man, except for a weighty reason.'"
Regarding the causes and conditions: wild beasts and various perils—these are called the great causes and conditions.
(100) "Sisters! The rules of training for the community have already been recited."
Now I ask: "Are you all pure in this matter, sisters?
A second and third time he speaks thus: "Sisters, since you are silent, you are pure in this matter; let it be so held."

"Sisters, the introduction to the Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa has been recited; the eight pārājika rules have been recited; the seventeen saṃghāvaśeṣa rules have been recited; the thirty naiḥsargika-pāyattika rules have been recited; the two hundred and ten pāyattika rules have been recited; the eight pratideśanīya rules have been recited; and the śaikṣa training rules have been recited."
This Dharma is included within the Buddha’s Sūtra on the Precepts, recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa,
as well as other dharmas that follow the Path.
Regarding this, all you sisters, with one mind, in harmony and joy, without contention— like water and milk blending together— dwell in peace and happiness.
"You should train yourselves thus.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, for the sake of the Saṅgha of those seeking tranquility, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"Patience is the supreme path; Nirvāṇa is declared by the Buddha to be foremost."
"One who causes affliction to others while having left the household life is not called a śramaṇa.
Thus did Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, briefly proclaim the Prātimokṣa for the silent saṃgha:
"Just as a person with clear vision is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths,"
"In this world there are wise people who are able to distance themselves from all evils.
Thus did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipasyin briefly proclaim the Prātimokṣa for the silent Saṅgha:
"Do not harm others, do not speak of their faults; act according to what is taught in the precepts."
"Eating with moderation, always delighting in secluded places,
with a tranquil mind rejoicing in diligence— this is called the teaching of the Buddhas.
Thus did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda briefly proclaim the Prātimokṣa for the silent Saṅgha:
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, taking its nectar without harming its color or fragrance,
so too should one go among the families,
not destroying others' affairs and regardless of what has been done or left undone."
"Only observe your own conduct, And discern clearly what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Konāgamana, for the sake of the Saṅgha of tranquility, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa:
"If you wish to attain a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; You should diligently train in the wholesome Dharma of the Noble Ones."
"If there is one who knows how to dwell in silent single-mindedness, Then they shall have no further sorrow or affliction.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, briefly proclaimed the Prātimokṣa for the silent Saṅgha:
"Commit no evil whatsoever, And fully cultivate all wholesome dharmas;
"Purify your own mind; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
Thus did the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni briefly proclaim the Prātimokṣa for the Saṅgha of the Peaceful Ones:
"To guard the body is good; to guard the speech is also good."
It is good to guard the mind; it is also good to guard all [the senses].
A bhikkhu who guards all [the senses] shall be freed from all suffering.
A bhikkhu who restrains his speech and mind, and whose body commits no evil, [is truly guarded].
These three paths of action are pure; one attains the path realized by the noble ones.

If a person strikes or reviles you, do not retaliate; harbor no resentment toward those who feel hatred, and let your mind always remain pure toward those who are angry; when you see others committing evil, do not do it yourself.
“The Seven Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, who are able to rescue and protect the world, have fully proclaimed the Sūtra of Precepts; I have now extensively explained it.
All Buddhas and their disciples revere this Sūtra of Precepts.”
"Having honored the Sūtra of the Precepts, and each showing mutual respect,
being fully endowed with shame and remorse, one can attain the unconditioned Way. "Sisters!"
The Prātimokṣa has been fully recited; the Saṃgha, being of one mind, has performed the Poṣadha.
— *Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, Section Five.
